checkpoints: The stateless design encodes a payload of {userId, channel, category, exp} and signs it with HMAC-SHA256, producing a token of the form payload.signature.
Verification recomputes the signature from the received payload and compares it in constant time, authenticating identity without ever touching the database.
Because exp sits inside the signed bytes, tampering with it to extend the token's life breaks the signature immediately — the token's expiry cannot be forged.

What stateless buys you: zero database lookup at verify time, self-expiring behavior from the embedded exp, nothing to store or clean up, and trivial horizontal scaling since any server holding the secret can verify.
The cost of stateless: you cannot revoke one specific issued token individually.
The classic failure scenario: a user unsubscribes and later re-subscribes, but an old, still-unexpired token (sitting in an old email) can flip their preference back off.

The fix is to embed a preferenceVersion claim that increments on every re-subscribe and reject tokens whose version predates the user's current version — this restores per-token revocation at the cost of one database read.

The alternative design — a random token stored in the database — inverts the trade-off (true per-token revocation and single-use enforcement, but every verify is a database lookup plus a cleanup job for expired rows); recommendation: stateless for high-volume, short-lived, low-risk marketing links, stored tokens where single-use must be strictly guaranteed, such as a link carrying financial value.
A resolved send call and its messageId only prove that the SMTP server returned 250 OK — the relay took custody of the message and accepted it for onward delivery.
That is not the same claim as 'the recipient's inbox has it' — the actual outcome is decided later, asynchronously, by mail servers the sending system does not control.

The truth arrives as a bounce report, routed back either through the envelope's MAIL FROM return-path or pushed by the delivery provider's event webhook (SES SNS, SendGrid Event), well after the original send already resolved.
A permanent bounce (address does not exist) goes straight onto a suppression list and is never sent to again.
A transient bounce (mailbox full, greylisting) gets bounded retries instead of immediate suppression — it is not treated the same as a permanent bounce.
Consulting that suppression list before every future send is a correctness feature, not a nice-to-have — it keeps the system honest about which addresses are actually reachable.

This is a different guarantee entirely from a startup connectivity check on the mail sender, which only fails fast on a bad host or bad credentials and says nothing about whether any individual future message will be delivered.

The stakes: receiving providers score sending domains, and a domain that keeps hammering addresses it already knows are dead looks like a spammer — reputation decays for the whole domain, not just the one address, so legitimate transactional email starts landing in spam or getting rejected, and recovery is slow.

A check-then-act sequence built from separate GET, compare, and INCR calls is not atomic as a whole, even though each individual Redis command such as INCR is atomic on its own — atomicity of one step does not compose into atomicity of the sequence around it.

When many concurrent requests each GET the same attempts counter before any of their INCR calls has landed, they all read the same stale, pre-increment value and all pass the same gate check — this is exactly why firing 50 parallel wrong-code requests against one identifier lets nearly all of them through instead of 5.

Deferring the increment until after the code comparison (which takes real time, including a timing-safe buffer compare) widens the race window: a slow verify step gives the whole concurrent burst more time to read the stale counter and slip past the limit before it updates.

Moving the atomic INCR to the very start of the flow and using its own return value as the gate closes the race, because INCR is a single read-modify-write step on Redis's event loop — concurrent callers get back distinct, strictly increasing integers, so no two callers can ever see the same count and both proceed.

Gating on the value INCR returns also means only requests within the allowed limit ever reach the expensive code comparison, so attackers can no longer burn free comparison attempts by piling requests into the slow verify window.

Splitting counter creation and its expiry into two separate round trips — an INCR followed later by a conditional EXPIRE — leaves a crash window: if the process dies or errors between the two calls, the counter key persists in storage with no TTL, producing a permanent lockout for that identifier.

Pairing counter creation and expiry atomically, either through a server-side script (e.g. a Lua script via defineCommand) that does INCR then conditional EXPIRE in one atomic execution, or through a SET ... NX EX seed for the first attempt followed by plain INCR afterward, guarantees the counter can never exist without an expiry attached.

Verifying the fix requires a concurrency test that fires many parallel wrong-code requests against a single identifier and asserts that at most the configured max-attempts count reach the comparison logic, plus a separate test that simulates a crash between the increment and expiry calls and confirms the key still expires within the window rather than living forever.

A stateless unsubscribe token carries no server-side record of its own existence — the HMAC signature appended to the payload is the entire proof of authenticity, not a lookup key into a database row.

Because `verifyToken()` recomputes `createHmac("sha256", cfg.secret).update(payloadB64)` and compares it against the signature already embedded in the token, that comparison only succeeds when `cfg.secret` is the exact value that was active when `sign()` originally minted the token.

Old-email links returning 403 while new-email links return 200, with the failure onset lining up exactly with the deploy timestamp, points at the signing key material rather than a logic bug in `sign()` or `verifyToken()` — a real code regression would misbehave regardless of when the token was issued.

Rotating `NOTIFICATION_SECRET` changes `cfg.secret` for every request going forward, so every signature computed with the old secret before the deploy can never match a recomputation with the new secret again — the mismatch is total and instantaneous the moment the new secret is loaded.

Because there is no token table to migrate, the outage isn't a data-consistency problem to backfill; it's a direct, permanent consequence of the signature being cryptographically bound to whichever secret produced it, and it persists for the full remaining `tokenTtlSeconds` (7 days) since nothing about an individual token expires early just because the secret rotated.

The fix is a dual-secret acceptance window: change `NotificationConfig.secret: string` to `secrets: string[]` (newest first), have `sign()` mint only with `secrets[0]`, and have `verifyToken()` iterate over the full list — recomputing the HMAC and checking `timingSafeEqual` against each candidate — so both the new and the previous secret verify successfully during the transition.

The old secret should only be dropped from the accepted list once the longest possible outstanding token (up to a full `tokenTtlSeconds` after the rotation) has expired; retiring it earlier would reproduce the same outage for tokens still in flight.

If the secret was rotated because it was genuinely compromised rather than as routine hygiene, keeping it in the accept-list to preserve backward compatibility re-exposes the leaked key, so the outage for that cohort of tokens may need to be accepted rather than bridged.

Alerting on the `403 INVALID_SIGNATURE` rate for any deploy that touches the signing secret would surface a rotation-caused outage within minutes instead of relying on a flood of support tickets to notice it.

Implicit TLS is the mode associated with the well-known port 465, while port 587 is the STARTTLS submission port that expects a plain connection which upgrades to TLS in-band after the initial handshake.

Setting `secure: true` together with `port: 587` creates a contradiction: the client opens an implicit-TLS handshake immediately while a server listening on 587 waits for a plain connection first, so against a real mail relay the handshake either hangs waiting for a TLS ClientHello or fails outright.

A permissive local SMTP stub like MailHog accepts connections regardless of TLS mode, so it never surfaces the port/TLS mismatch — the bug only becomes visible once the code is pointed at a real relay such as SendGrid, SES, or Gmail.
Building a brand-new Nodemailer transporter inside `sendWelcome` on every call means each email pays the cost of a fresh TCP-plus-TLS handshake instead of reusing an already-open connection.
The transporter should be constructed once — for example through a `useFactory` provider — and injected as a shared singleton, so every send reuses the same connection and any pooling it provides.

Hardcoding the SMTP host and the `from` address as string literals inside the method body means moving from a local stub to a staging or production relay requires editing source code rather than changing configuration.

SMTP host, credentials, and the sender identity belong in environment-driven configuration (e.g. read through `ConfigService`/`registerAs`), the same pattern the rest of the module's config follows, so the code stays identical across environments.

Without a `transporter.verify()` call at startup or in a health check, invalid credentials or an unreachable SMTP host only surface the first time a real user triggers `sendWelcome`, instead of failing the application boot.

Passing local tests or working against a stub inbox only proves the stub is forgiving — it does not prove the SMTP configuration is correct against a real provider, so 'it runs in MailHog' is not sufficient evidence to approve the PR.
Validation belongs at the multipart-parsing layer because that is where the bytes first arrive, before the handler ever runs — the fail-fast model.
A fileSize limit applied mid-stream aborts the transfer the moment the cap is exceeded, avoiding wasted disk/RAM.
A type filter at that same layer rejects a disallowed MIME before the handler runs.
The client-declared mimetype is just the Content-Type header of the multipart part and is entirely client-controlled — a renamed .exe sent as image/jpeg passes this check.
The allow-list is only a first gate; production adds magic-byte checking on top, reading the leading bytes against binary signatures (e.g., Go's http.DetectContentType does this out of the box).
When the parser rejects, it throws its own error class rather than the framework's standard HTTP exception, so default error handling would return a generic 500.

A dedicated central mapping point (e.g., an exception filter) translates the size-limit error into 413 and the filtered-out MIME into 415 with a standard body, applied globally so every upload route stays consistent.

Flow: the client asks the API for a URL with filename/content-type; the server generates a key and uses its secret key to HMAC-SHA256-sign a canonical request (method + bucket + key + timestamp + TTL + signed headers).
The signature and parameters are embedded directly in the URL's query string, so the URL alone carries everything needed to authorize the request.

The client then PUTs the file bytes straight to storage — the application server never touches the data path, and since authorization is carried entirely by the URL, the server's credentials never leave it either.
Storage independently recomputes the signature: a tampered parameter, a changed signed header, or an expired TTL all cause a mismatch and return 403 Forbidden.
The URL authorizes exactly one operation on one key for a short window.
Upload (PUT) and download (GET) are signed at two separate endpoints because they represent different permission sets, whose authorization rules and TTLs can differ per direction.

A resumable upload protocol like tus allows a client to pause and resume a transfer hours or even days after creation, so any auth check performed only when the upload is created captures a token whose validity has nothing to do with when the resume actually happens.

Guarding only the POST (creation) handler while leaving PATCH and HEAD unguarded means the resume path — which is the entire point of resumable uploads — has no authentication at all, letting anyone who knows the upload id push chunks or probe its state.

Simply reusing the creation-time token on later PATCH/HEAD requests does not fix the gap either: by the time a real resume happens, hours or days later, that token is very likely expired, so the guard would just reject every genuine resume with a 401.

The correct fix is to require fresh authentication on every state-mutating request (and any request that can leak upload existence or offset), checked against a token supplied per-request, paired with a refresh path the client can call before resuming.

Wiring a tus handler in as a normal NestJS @Controller route means it runs through the exact same request pipeline as every other endpoint, including any global body parser (such as bodyParser.json()) registered in main.ts ahead of all controllers.

A tus PATCH request carries Content-Type: application/offset+octet-stream — a raw binary chunk, not JSON — so routing it through a JSON body-parsing pipeline before the tus handler sees it can silently truncate or corrupt the byte stream.

The structural fix is to register the tus server as raw middleware (e.g. NestMiddleware with RequestMethod.ALL) mounted ahead of the framework's controller pipeline on both the collection path and the per-upload path, so the untouched request and response reach the tus handler before any body parser runs, with the auth check placed inside that same middleware so it applies to every verb.

A demo can pass cleanly while both structural flaws remain invisible: a short test upload finishes in seconds, well inside the token's lifetime, and a small or simple payload can pass through the parsing pipeline without visibly breaking — neither bug surfaces until a real, long-lived, multi-chunk resume is exercised.

Verifying the fix requires two targeted tests: one that lets the token expire mid-upload and asserts the resumed request is freshly re-authenticated rather than silently succeeding or always failing, and one that asserts the stored file is byte-for-byte identical to the source after a multi-chunk upload, which would fail if any parsing step had touched the stream.

The finalize routine performs two full passes over the payload: pass one reads every chunk file completely into memory and then writes it to the destination file, and pass two reopens that assembled file and streams it end to end solely to compute a hash — for an N-byte upload that totals two full reads plus one full write.
Doubling the read I/O this way is exactly why a 1 GB finalize takes roughly twice as long as a true single-pass merge would.

Loading each chunk with a whole-file read before writing it out means peak memory during the merge loop equals one full chunk's size per iteration, so memory usage scales up with whatever chunk size the service happens to be configured with instead of staying flat.

A hash object is stateful and can be updated incrementally: calling `hash.update()` on each buffer as it streams through the existing per-chunk merge loop, right before that same buffer is piped or written to the destination, lets the checksum finish alongside the merge instead of requiring a second dedicated pass.

Collapsing merge and hashing into one streaming pass removes the second full read of the file and replaces whole-chunk buffering with small, constant-size stream buffers, so both wall-time and peak memory stop scaling with chunk size or total file size.

Restructuring the I/O this way doesn't change the correctness invariants: chunks must still be merged in strict `0..N-1` order, because both the assembled file bytes and the running hash are order-sensitive, so merging chunks out of order or in parallel would corrupt the output and invalidate the checksum.

The completeness check — comparing the number of received chunks against the expected total — must still run before any I/O starts, and cleanup of the temp chunk directory must still happen only after the merge has actually succeeded.

Computing the checksum only at finalize time accepts a deliberate trade-off: corruption is detected only after the entire upload has been merged, rather than the moment a bad chunk arrives. A per-chunk checksum, like the one in the tus protocol's checksum extension, would catch a bad chunk earlier, but at the cost of extra hashing work on every single chunk request — overhead that isn't justified for a lesson-scale upload service.

Multer's default `FileInterceptor` uses memory storage, so the entire file is already sitting in `file.buffer` before the handler body runs; re-uploading that same buffer through `PutObjectCommand` doubles the bandwidth per upload, since bytes cross two legs — client→server, then server→storage.

Per-request RAM cost is roughly equal to the uploaded file's size, so N concurrent uploads hold N × filesize in heap at the same time — this is why OOM tracks concurrency under load, not average traffic volume.

The request holds an event-loop tick and the underlying connection for the full duration of the transfer (seconds to minutes for large files), which makes the API tier's connection/thread capacity — not CPU — the real throughput ceiling, and explains why P99 balloons under concurrent load.

Removing the server from the data path means replacing the proxy handler with a presign endpoint: the server generates a collision-free key and signs a short-TTL PUT URL via `getSignedUrl` with `PutObjectCommand`, the client PUTs the bytes directly to S3/MinIO, and storage validates the HMAC-SHA256 signature itself — server cost per upload drops from the full transfer time to sub-millisecond signing, with no buffer and no held connection.

Since a presign endpoint with no auth check would sign URLs for anyone who asks, authentication has to move into a guard that runs before `createUploadUrl` is called, rather than being implicit in the old handler.

A declared `size` field on the presign request is otherwise unsigned and uncapped for the whole TTL window, so it must be validated server-side on the request DTO to re-establish the size limit the old buffering handler enforced implicitly.

Signing `ContentType` as part of the presigned request causes a mismatched `Content-Type` header on the client's PUT to be rejected with 403 by storage, restoring the type check the proxy handler used to perform before forwarding to S3.

The bucket's CORS policy must explicitly allow `PUT` from the client's origin, or a browser's direct upload fails before a single byte reaches MinIO/S3 — a requirement that didn't exist when the server was proxying every request.

Because a completed request through the old handler used to double as proof that an upload happened, taking the server out of the data path introduces a new failure mode: a client that never confirms leaves an orphan object in storage, which needs a confirmation callback or a lifecycle rule on a `temp/` key prefix to clean up.
